PullRequest.Title: Files: keep disk watch requests in sets
PullRequest.Body:

* Read our Pull Request guidelines:

`AbstractDiskFileSystemProvider` kept its universal and non-recursive watch requests in arrays. Removing a request used `arrays.remove` (`indexOf` and `splice`), which is quadratic when many watchers come and go. That happens when the TypeScript server, started with `--canUseWatchEvents`, makes the TypeScript extension create and dispose one file watcher per watched file or folder while a project loads.

This PR keeps the requests in `Set`s: adding and removing are constant time, and the watchers get `Array.from(set)`.

No issue is associated; this came from profiling.

## Measured on my machine

Code OSS dev build, TypeScript language features in a clone of this repository; window CPU profile:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `arrays.remove` from the watch request removers | 160 ms | 0 ms |
| All time in `diskFileSystemProvider` | 471 ms | 265 ms |

## Why behavior is unchanged

- A `Set` iterates in insertion order, and `delete` leaves the other entries in place, the same as `push` followed by `indexOf` and `splice`.
- Each `watch` call creates its own request object, and each disposable removes only that object. So two equal requests from two calls stay two separate entries, as before.
- The watchers now receive a copy instead of the live array. They don't change it. The universal watcher client keeps the last array it received in order to restart after an error. A restart while a refresh is still pending now replays the last requests it was sent, and the pending refresh then sends the current ones, so no update is lost.

## How to test

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `node build/next/index.ts transpile` | passed |
| `./scripts/test.sh --run src/vs/platform/files/test/node/diskFileSystemProvider.test.ts` | passed, 22 passing, 0 failing |
| `node_modules/.bin/tsc --project ./src/tsconfig.json --noEmit --skipLibCheck` | passed |
| `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/vs/platform/files/common/diskFileSystemProvider.ts` | passed |

No test is added: the watchers end up with the same requests in the same order as before, and a test of request order passes with the old code too. The tests above don't call `watch` on the provider. A throwaway script with fake watcher clients, run against the old and new compiled code, sent the same requests in the same order; the only difference was the restart replay described above.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: Disposing N distinct universal watch requests called arrays.remove N times over a shrinking array. indexOf and splice perform collection-sized search and/or shifts even though refresh work is coalesced, yielding O(N^2) synchronous CPU during large project watcher churn.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: Strong static evidence of synchronous quadratic CPU work on desktop window watcher disposal for large TypeScript projects; it competes with the window event loop. No benchmark was independently executed.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: Identity-based Set.add/delete makes collection maintenance expected constant time per request, avoiding quadratic synchronous disposal work. Array.from is performed only at the existing debounced/throttled refresh, whose 0/500 ms delays and one-active-plus-coalesced-pending execution remain unchanged.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: The deleted base line 88 used insert(this.universalWatchRequests, request); its returned remover was called synchronously on disposal at base line 97. arrays.ts:488-505 implements this as push followed by indexOf and splice. typescriptServiceClient.ts:1057-1089 creates/closes watchers from TypeScript server events; mainThreadFileSystemEventService.ts:258-268 forwards watch/unwatch to FileService. FileService.doWatch:1295-1325 reference-counts identical URI/options but retains distinct requests, so thousands of distinct files can still reach this collection. The desktop provider forces all requests through the universal collection (electron-browser/diskFileSystemProvider.ts:43). Each removal scans and/or shifts the remaining collection, producing quadratic aggregate CPU for disposing a large batch. The changed RIGHT line 96 uses Set.delete instead. blame_base_line(88) identifies commit 7dd4d72fcb35508f9ec1b8575c240513856bb972.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: Repeated synchronous indexOf/splice removals over the non-recursive request array make bulk disposal quadratic in the number of distinct provider-level requests, blocking the owning node/session event loop even though downstream refreshes are throttled.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: Large batches of non-recursive watcher disposal consume quadratic CPU and delay other work on the node provider's event loop. This is established from the call path and array implementation, not independently measured timing.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: Replaces linear array removal with expected constant-time Set.delete per request. Full request arrays are materialized only for existing throttled refreshes, preserving watch order, object identity, and downstream deduplication.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: The deleted base line 182 used insert(this.nonRecursiveWatchRequests, request), and its remover ran synchronously on every last-reference disposal at base line 190. arrays.ts:488-505 shows insert returns a remover using array.indexOf plus splice. AbstractDiskFileSystemProvider.watch:59-64 routes non-recursive requests here unless forceUniversal is set; node/diskFileSystemProvider.ts:993-998 supplies the in-process NodeJSWatcherClient, and AbstractSessionFileWatcher:305,335-351 creates a node provider per IPC session and disposes its watch requests. FileService:1295-1325 deduplicates identical URI/options, not large sets of distinct paths. Therefore bulk removal of N effective requests performs O(N^2) collection maintenance regardless of the coalesced refresh. RIGHT line 189 now deletes the object from a Set. blame_base_line(182) returns introducing commit 32111287f061d8c435b059aeba8c2de5ad71e8d1.

Scenarios.Scenario: Desktop TypeScript project load/reload, watcher churn, and bulk disposal through the forced universal watcher
Scenarios.CriticalPath: TypeScript create/close events reach main-thread FileService.watch/unwatch. Provider request insertion/removal is synchronous on the window event loop; actual watcher activation is deferred. A refresh waits for the unchanged debounce (0 ms or 500 ms above 200 requests), worker availability, and the watch RPC. TypeScript's watch API returns without waiting for activation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Extension-host watcher registration/disposal reaches the main-thread FileService.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One registration/disposal message per extension watcher; FileService then coalesces identical URI/options into a single provider request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same extension watch/unwatch messages and FileService deduplication occurred before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Precedes provider request maintenance but does not wait for complete backend watcher readiness.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Acquire the utility-process file-watcher worker and channel.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One acquisition per lazily initialized client, plus bounded error restarts; not one process per watched file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same lazy worker acquisition and reuse.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The first refresh's RPC waits for the delayed channel; warm refreshes reuse it.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create the request array and send the full request list through the watcher proxy.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shallow N-reference Array.from allocation per coalesced refresh is new; one existing RPC serializes the N requests per refresh, not one RPC per entry.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Passed the live request array without the shallow copy. Full-list RPC serialization and refresh scheduling already existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Snapshot creation runs synchronously at refresh execution; transport and watch completion hold the active refresh slot.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stat new paths, reuse recursive subscriptions when possible, otherwise resolve real paths and open fs.watch; enumerate newly watched directories.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Stat once per newly started effective non-recursive watcher; additional realpath/fs.watch and directory readdir only when needed. Unchanged active watchers are retained, and duplicate paths within each correlation group collapse.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same effective request set, deduplication, recursive reuse, chunking, and filesystem operations.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Backend setup enables events asynchronously; chunking prevents all watcher constructors from running in one synchronous burst.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N distinct provider-level URI/options requests after FileService's hash-based reference counting; thousands of distinct files are explicitly supported. Duplicate consumers do not each create a provider entry. Downstream non-recursive requests are further grouped by correlation and normalized path.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One universal provider ThrottledDelayer permits one active refresh and one coalesced pending task; repeated triggers reset the debounce as before. UniversalWatcher configures recursive requests before non-recursive requests. NodeJSWatcher starts up to 100 new watchers per work chunk with 100 ms rests; asynchronous filesystem setup can overlap across chunks.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: FileService reuses identical active requests until their final release. The watcher client is lazily created once and reused. Existing backend watchers survive unchanged refreshes. The new Set preserves separate request object identities and order, while a refresh creates one shallow N-element snapshot. The client retains only its last snapshot, not an accumulating history.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: traced TypeScript create/close handlers, main-thread forwarding, FileService reference counting, desktop forceUniversal routing, debounce/throttler, worker acquisition, and backend reuse. Set deletion removes the previous collection-wide removal cost.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No independent profile was run. Actual N and refresh frequency depend on project size, request reuse, and event timing; the shallow-copy cost is unmeasured.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced high-confidence regression. Expected constant-time identity deletion replaces synchronous indexOf/splice. The new O(N) shallow copy occurs once per already-coalesced full-list refresh, with no additional RPCs, processes, or watcher fan-out. Recorded the concrete removal-cost fix and its blamed introducing commit.

Scenarios.Scenario: Node/session non-recursive watching, warm updates, and teardown of a large watch session
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Existing DiskFileSystemProviderClient watch/unwatch calls reach a per-session node provider. Request maintenance is synchronous in the receiving event loop; backend refresh and activation are deferred through the same provider delayer. Session teardown synchronously disposes outstanding request handles, then disposes its provider.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send watch/unwatch requests through the existing channel to the session provider and return file-change events.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One call per effective client registration or disposal; session-level grouping owns one provider, not one provider per request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same per-request IPC cardinality, per-session provider ownership, and event transport.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Messages precede receiver-side maintenance. Client watch returns a disposable without awaiting backend readiness.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Materialize Set entries as the array required by the in-process watcher client.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One O(N) shallow array per coalesced flush; no IPC is introduced by this conversion.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Passed the existing live array directly to the same in-process client.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous work during the deferred refresh, not during every insertion/removal.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stat, resolve, open/enumerate newly watched paths and close removed watcher handles.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Setup only for new or changed effective path/correlation keys; close only for removed/replaced active instances. Warm identical requests reuse existing instances.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same filesystem setup, instance reuse, handle closure, and session cleanup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for actual file-event coverage, but not awaited by the original watch API; creation remains chunked.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N distinct provider-level non-recursive requests per session; upstream FileService reference counting can reduce identical requests. Backend grouping further reduces this to distinct normalized paths per correlation group.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each provider has a non-recursive ThrottledDelayer separate from its universal delayer, with one active refresh and coalesced pending work. Sessions remain independent. Backend creation uses the existing 100-watcher chunks/100 ms rests, not a new unbounded synchronous constructor loop.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: One node DiskFileSystemProvider is retained per session, and one non-recursive client is created lazily on first flush. Its NodeJSWatcher map reuses unchanged active instances. Removed keys are deleted. The client holds one latest request snapshot; no per-refresh snapshot history is added. Direct node-only operation has no watch RPC.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: traced client/server/session ownership, node watcher creation, reference counting, grouping, and disposal. All lifecycle refresh triggers and throttling remain in place.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Session counts, distinct path counts, and filesystem latency vary. The asymptotic removal improvement is provable without timings.
Scenarios.Verdict: No high-confidence introduced regression. Set.delete removes quadratic bulk array-removal work while preserving refresh scheduling and downstream cardinality. Recorded this fix separately because blame identifies a different introducing commit.

Scenarios.Scenario: Recursive workspace watching and optional polling during initial activation and warm refresh
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The provider's universal refresh waits for its watcher RPC. UniversalWatcher awaits recursive configuration before non-recursive configuration. Recursive duplicate normalization and path validation precede stopping/starting changed backend watchers. This affects file-event readiness, not synchronous watch API return.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the full coalesced request list to the existing node subprocess or desktop utility worker.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One watch RPC per coalesced universal refresh; one lazily created watcher process per client, apart from bounded restarts.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same process topology and full-list RPC count. Only the producer-side shallow snapshot is new.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: RPC completion gates the provider's next active refresh.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Validate candidate roots with stat/lstat, normalize real paths/casing, subscribe or unsubscribe native recursive watchers.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Checks scale with grouped candidate roots and overlap checks; subscriptions only for new/changed surviving roots. Existing root watchers are reused.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical validation, root grouping, overlap suppression, and native watcher reuse.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Validation and awaited native setup are on recursive event-readiness and refresh completion paths.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Write snapshot files, read changes since the prior snapshot, and unlink snapshots on disposal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: For configured polling only: one snapshot write per effective root per cycle, one getEventsSince after the first cycle, and one cleanup unlink per stopped root.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same opt-in polling roots, snapshot operations, timing, and cleanup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Initial snapshot establishes polling readiness; subsequent scans run on unchanged scheduled intervals.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: R recursive provider requests, grouped by correlation and normalized path, then reduced for overlapping roots unless symbolic links require preserving children. New native subscriptions scale with changed surviving roots, not all files within those roots.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Provider refreshes are serialized/coalesced per universal client. ParcelWatcher validates requests and stops/starts native subscriptions using awaited loops. Polling schedules its next cycle after its current work. The PR does not change this ordering or concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Existing native watcher instances are reused when path/correlation and options match. Recursive path validation can repeat on refresh as before. Polling retains its existing per-root snapshot file and interval; the PR introduces no new polling cache or invalidation policy.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: inspected universal recursive-before-non-recursive ordering, recursive grouping, awaited start/stop loops, native subscription, normalization, and polling operations.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Workspace root count, symbolic-link overlaps, tree sizes for polling, and filesystem speeds are unknown; none changes due to Set conversion.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced performance regression: no increase in effective roots, validation frequency, native subscriptions, polling frequency, or process/IPC cardinality.

Scenarios.Scenario: Universal watcher recovery during a pending refresh, and failed/missing-path monitoring
Scenarios.CriticalPath: An eligible unexpected watcher error immediately initializes a replacement client backend and replays its saved request array; a pending provider refresh later supplies current requests. Individual failed requests do not cause whole-client restarts. Missing paths are suspended and monitored until reappearance or removal.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Reinitialize a failed watcher process/worker and replay saved watch requests via its proxy.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One reinitialization and watch replay per eligible error, capped at five; no new restart trigger or cap change.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same restart operations and cap, but replay observed the mutable live provider array rather than the last submitted snapshot.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required to resume event coverage after an actual watcher failure; a pending normal refresh can subsequently reconcile current requests.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Reuse a recursive subscription or monitor a missing path through fs.watchFile; unwatch it on removal or resumption.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One monitor per distinct suspended request ID, with polling fallback at the existing interval when recursive reuse is unavailable.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same suspension, reuse, polling interval, request-ID deduplication, and disposal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Keeps missing paths off normal active-watcher setup until reappearance; resumed setup uses existing update scheduling.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: At most five whole-client error restarts per client lifetime. A restart replays the last submitted N-entry snapshot rather than the live collection. Failed-path monitoring scales with distinct suspended request IDs after backend grouping, not every duplicated caller.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Error restart replay exists outside the provider delayer both before and after the change. Normal pending refreshes remain serialized/coalesced; backend watcher refreshes use their existing delayers. Non-recursive creation remains chunked. Failed-path fallback uses the existing 5007 ms fs.watchFile interval.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Before the PR, the saved array aliased the live provider collection; afterward it is the last submitted snapshot. This can temporarily retain or replay removed entries until a pending flush, but does not accumulate a history. Suspended requests are removed/disposed when absent from subsequent current requests; existing recursive subscriptions are preferred to polling.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the snapshot/restart behavior, lifetime bound, restart cap, and unchanged monitor path; insufficient evidence of an actionable performance regression from that error-only replay difference.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Unexpected process failures overlapping request churn are uncommon and their exact frequency is unknown. A stale snapshot may briefly recreate removed watches, but this requires recovery and is bounded by the saved batch/restart cap; no independent timing data establishes a material regression.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable high-confidence regression. Snapshot semantics differ during recovery, but there is no accumulating history, increased normal-path call count, changed retry policy, or new unbounded retention. Did not report correctness-only replay/state considerations.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance-review pass over the entire one-file inventory and all ten diff hunks. Traced callers, identity/refcount deduplication, refresh coalescing, process/IPC boundaries, filesystem setup, backend reuse, snapshot ownership, failure recovery, and teardown. No high-confidence introduced performance findings. Submitted two internal regression-fix signals for the proven quadratic array-removal mechanisms, with distinct introducing commits resolved through base blame. Static read-only review; no performance measurements independently executed.
